visuals.caption: 1️⃣ Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
visuals.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    participant DB as Database
    
    Note over App: Read Request
    App->>Cache: GET user:123
    
    alt Cache Hit
        Cache-->>App: Return cached data (1ms)
    else Cache Miss
        Cache-->>App: NULL
        App->>DB: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=123
        DB-->>App: Return user data (50ms)
        App->>Cache: SET user:123, data
        App-->>App: Return user data
    end
    
    Note over App: Write Request
    App->>DB: UPDATE users SET name='John'
    DB-->>App: OK
    App->>Cache: DEL user:123
    Note over Cache: Next read will fetch fresh data

visuals.caption: Solution 1: Request Coalescing (Single Flight)
visuals.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant R1 as Request 1
    participant R2 as Request 2-1000
    participant Lock as Single Flight Lock
    participant Cache
    participant DB
    
    R1->>Lock: Acquire lock
    Lock-->>R1: Granted
    R1->>DB: Query database
    
    R2->>Lock: Try acquire lock
    Lock-->>R2: Wait...
    
    DB-->>R1: Return data
    R1->>Cache: SET feed:homepage
    R1->>Lock: Release lock
    R1-->>R1: Return data
    
    Lock-->>R2: Proceed
    R2->>Cache: GET feed:homepage
    Cache-->>R2: Return cached data ✅

visuals.caption: READ COMMITTED sees only committed changes and is PostgreSQL's default; READ UNCOMMITTED can see uncommitted changes and is rarely used; REPEATABLE READ keeps repeated reads consistent; SERIALIZABLE is strongest and catches write skew by aborting one transaction.

Zero-row writes are not errors, so check counts and roll back before inserts; Wrong guarded row means a counter cannot prove seat A15 is free; Locking too long should be fixed by narrow millisecond locks and no payment calls inside transactions; Deadlocks are prevented with globally sorted lock order and retried aborts; ABA problem is fixed with a dedicated incrementing version; Distributed lock overuse should be avoided when one database transaction is enough.

Redis with TTL uses SET NX plus TTL for fast auto-expiring locks but can overlap if the holder stalls; Database columns use reserved_by and reserved_until with no new infrastructure; ZooKeeper/etcd provide strong consensus coordination but add operational complexity.
Seat checkout hold uses 10 minutes while the user enters payment details; Ride request hold uses 10 seconds before a stale pending_request reads as free.
Upload options: Presigned URLs are the default for most large uploads; Chunked uploads resume failed chunks; Server as Proxy is only for byte inspection.
Download options: CDN signed URLs give fast delivery with edge validation and caching; Blob storage signatures are simpler for infrequent downloads; Range requests allow resumable downloads.
Presigned URL TTL: typically 15 minutes to 1 hour.
Upload size limits: S3 parts are 5MB-5GB; Azure blocks are 4MB-100MB.
Upload transfer time: at 100 Mbps, a 5 GB video takes 429 seconds, or 7 minutes 9 seconds.
Incomplete upload cleanup window: delete incomplete multipart uploads after 24-48 hours.

State sync: Pending metadata rows are created before files exist; Event notifications are the primary sync path; Reconciliation jobs catch delayed or lost events; Client completion should not be trusted.
Signature-level controls: content-length-range caps upload size; content-type enforces expected types; Server-chosen keys prevent overwrites.
Post-upload inspection: Quarantine buckets hold uploads before public access; Content analysis scans and validates files.

Provider names: AWS uses Presigned URLs, Multipart Upload API, S3 Event Notifications, CloudFront, and Lifecycle Rules; Google Cloud uses Signed URLs, Resumable Uploads, Cloud Storage Pub/Sub, Cloud CDN, and Lifecycle Management; Azure uses SAS tokens, Block Blobs, Event Grid, Azure CDN, and Lifecycle Management Policies.

Kafka is the default interview pick unless constraints apply, with replay, fan-out, retention, huge volume, and partition ordering. Redis with Bull or BullMQ is startup-friendly with retries, delayed jobs, and priorities, but has memory-first durability tradeoffs. AWS SQS is managed and scalable with guaranteed delivery, but its 1 MB limit means passing IDs instead of full job data. RabbitMQ supports complex routing and enterprise workflows, but self-hosting adds cluster, upgrade, and disk monitoring work.

Normal servers are the default for interviews, giving full control, easy debugging, and support for long jobs. Serverless functions autoscale and charge per execution, but have cold starts and minimal local storage. Container-based workers on Kubernetes or ECS are more complex than servers but more flexible than serverless.
Quick profile query takes less than 0.1 seconds. PDF report generation takes at least 45 seconds in the example.
Web timeout limits are often 30 to 60 seconds. Function limit for serverless execution is 15 to 60 minutes depending on provider.

Worker crash is handled with heartbeats so the queue retries when the worker stops checking in. Duplicate work is prevented with idempotency keys that return the existing job ID. Queue overload is handled with depth limits and system busy responses. Mixed workloads need separate fast and slow queues to avoid blocking. Job dependencies can chain simple steps or use Step Functions, Temporal, or Airflow for complex workflows.

Saga Pattern uses local commits and unwinds earlier effects on later failure; Event-Driven Choreography uses durable-log events and works for mid-complexity but hides the flow; Workflow Orchestration uses one coordinator and fits complex flows needing control and visibility; Two-Phase Commit is a poor fit for long workflows because locks wait on the slowest participant and external systems may not support it.

Temporal is the most powerful open-source option with code-driven workflows, long waits, full history, and self-operation or Temporal Cloud; AWS Step Functions is a managed serverless state machine with standard runs capped at one year and 256KB between states; Durable Functions is an Azure cloud-native option that is easier to operate than Temporal but less flexible; Google Cloud Workflows is a cloud-native option similar to Durable Functions; Apache Airflow is strong for scheduled batch ETL but weaker for user-facing long-running workflows.

Workflow is deterministic high-level flow that must replay the same from inputs and history; Activity is one side-effecting step such as a service call, card charge, database read, or email; History Database is an append-only log of workflow decisions and Activity results; Replay recovers by re-executing from the top and returning recorded Activity results without re-running them; Temporal Server hands out tasks, tracks timeouts, records progress, and never runs your code.

Workflow Versioning keeps old executions on old code and new executions on new code, which is simple but not immediate; Workflow Migrations update the definition in place so running executions can pick up the change; patched() is a deterministic branch where old histories stay legacy and new arrivals run new behavior; Step Functions Pinning keeps running executions on their starting definition and applies updates only to new executions.

In-Memory Progress loses what happened after a crash unless progress is persisted outside the host; Callback Routing means a webhook may hit a different API server, so load persisted state or wake the workflow by ID; Manual State Machines leave database rows passive and lead to hand-rolled pollers, locks, retries, and claiming.

Compensating Actions undo committed steps in reverse and need retries and idempotency too; Idempotency Key records IN_PROGRESS before and COMPLETED after irreversible work and reconciles uncertain cases; Signals wake workflows by ID without holding a thread or worker memory; Continue-as-New starts a fresh run with current state and empty history; Activity Payloads should pass identifiers instead of huge inputs and results to keep history small.

Client protocols: Simple Polling is the default unless low latency is required, Long Polling holds HTTP requests for infrequent near-real-time updates, Server-Sent Events is a one-way HTTP stream, WebSockets is a full-duplex persistent channel, and WebRTC is peer-to-peer with signaling, STUN, and TURN.
Load balancers: L4 Load Balancer routes by IP and port while preserving TCP sessions, and L7 Load Balancer terminates connections and routes by HTTP content.

Connection pitfalls: HTTP keep-alive should exceed the polling interval, long-poll timeouts must align across every hop, streaming proxies can buffer SSE responses, and deployment churn forces persistent sockets to reconnect.

Trigger models: Pushing via Pub/Sub is the default for most real-time designs, Pushing via Consistent Hashes gives a predictable owner for heavy connection state, and Pulling via Polling uses DB-backed reads with delay and extra DB load.
Bidirectional delivery scenarios: Instant messages need bidirectional delivery, and typing indicators and presence need bidirectional delivery.

High-volume fan-out scenarios: Live Comments use batching and hierarchical aggregation for high-volume fan-out during live events, and Live Dashboards and Analytics use one-way metric updates with aggregation intervals.

Consistency and conflict scenarios: CRDTs handle collaborative document editing character-update conflicts, and Operational Transforms handle collaborative document editing character-update conflicts.

Deep dive fixes: Heartbeats detect broken sockets, Missed update replay uses per-user queues or sequence numbers, Celebrity fan-out caches once and distributes through layers, and Message ordering sends related messages through one server or partition.
Indexing is the default first move for queried, joined, or sorted columns; denormalization stores redundant data to avoid joins; materialized views precompute expensive aggregations.
Read replicas send writes to the primary and reads to replicas but can lag; database sharding splits large datasets; geographic sharding stores regional data near users.
Application-level caching keeps popular data in Redis or Memcached between the app and DB; CDN and edge caching stores shared content globally but skips user-specific data.

Time-based expiration is simple but can serve stale data; write-through invalidation updates cache on writes with extra latency; write-behind invalidation queues work with a stale window; versioned keys avoid delete races but need version tracking.
Request coalescing combines same-key fetches so the backend gets one request per app server; cache key fanout stores copies under multiple keys to spread a hot key.

Probabilistic early refresh is smarter than locks because refresh chance rises near expiry while serving cached data; distributed locks serialize rebuilds but are fragile; background refresh keeps critical entries warm before expiration.
Bitly or URL shorteners should aggressively cache short-to-long mappings because URLs do not change; Ticketmaster should cache event details but not seat availability and use replicas for browsing.

Estimate write throughput and find the bottleneck before scaling; vertical scaling is the default first step, with 200 CPU cores and 10gigabit network interfaces not uncommon; avoid premature sharding, queues, or batching if hardware or tuning handles the load.

Write-optimized databases include append-only, time-series, log-structured, or column stores when writes dominate reads; Cassandra append-only handles 10,000+ writes per second via append-only commit log; traditional relational databases may handle 1,000 writes per second for the same work with in-place updates.
Horizontal sharding splits rows across shards for manageable write slices; vertical partitioning splits columns or tables by access pattern so hot metrics do not interfere with content.
Redis Cluster slots hash each key with CRC to a slot whose owner receives the write; consistent hashing maps keys to servers and is worth knowing for interviewer probes.

Application batching works when the app can replay from Kafka; intermediate batching can turn 100 likes in 1 minute into 1 write; database-layer flushing is a big-hammer option with Redis flushing every 100ms by default.
Pipeline aggregation processes high-volume data in stages and reduces volume at each step.
Broadcast/proxy nodes reduce fan-out for shared live data; shared live-comment updates go to M broadcast nodes instead of N viewers.

Split all keys uses a fixed k to reduce per-shard writes but increases data and reads by k; split hot keys dynamically can use 100 sub-keys each handling 1,000 likes per second; aggregatable metrics only applies to likes, views, counts, and balances but not user profiles.

Always check sub-keys is the default in production because readers find dynamic splits without announcements; announcing splits to readers is more efficient but complex because readers must learn the split before writers execute it.

    MostRecentlyUsed --> LeastRecentlyUsed: other keys accessed, node drifts toward tail
    LeastRecentlyUsed --> MostRecentlyUsed: get(key) moves node back to front
    LeastRecentlyUsed --> Evicted: over capacity, remove tail.prev
    MostRecentlyUsed --> Expired: currentTime past expiry
    LeastRecentlyUsed --> Expired: currentTime past expiry
    Expired --> [*]: removed on get or by janitor cleanup
    Evicted --> [*]

    R-->>G1: { allowed, remaining }
    G2->>R: EVAL token-bucket Lua (runs only after G1 finishes)
    R-->>G2: { allowed, remaining }

visuals.caption: 1. Bid Ordering and Strong Consistency
visuals.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Bidder Client
    participant BS as Bid Service
    participant R as Redis (Lua)
    participant K as Kafka
    participant PG as Postgres

    C->>BS: POST /bids { amount, idempotencyKey }
    BS->>BS: stamp server-side receive timestamp
    BS->>R: GET idempotency:{key}
    alt key exists
        R-->>BS: cached result
        BS-->>C: return original response
    else new request
        BS->>R: EVAL Lua (compare-and-set current_price)
        alt closed or too low
            R-->>BS: {0, reason}
            BS-->>C: 409 TOO_LOW / 410 AUCTION_CLOSED
        else accepted
            R-->>BS: {1, newPrice}
            BS->>K: produce BidAccepted (acks=all)
            K-->>BS: durably committed
            BS-->>C: 201 ACCEPTED { currentPrice }
            K->>PG: project accepted bid (async)
        end
    end

    [*] --> ACTIVE: POST /auctions
    ACTIVE --> ACTIVE: bid accepted (new highest, updates currentPrice)
    ACTIVE --> ACTIVE: bid within soft-close window (HINCRBY end_time +30s)
    ACTIVE --> ACTIVE: bid rejected (TOO_LOW, price unchanged)
    ACTIVE --> CLOSED: now past end_time (Closer acquires lease, CAS ACTIVE to CLOSED)
    CLOSED --> [*]: emit AUCTION_CLOSED (winnerId, finalPrice)

    note right of ACTIVE
        server-side timestamp is authoritative;
        end_time check is atomic with the
        price comparison inside the Lua script

visuals.caption: 1. Idempotency End-to-End
visuals.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Merchant Client
    participant P as Payment Service
    participant I as Idempotency Store
    participant PSP as PSP

    Note over C: generate UUID key once, store locally
    C->>P: POST /payments (key K)
    P->>I: INSERT key K ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    I-->>P: inserted (fresh) → IN_PROGRESS
    P->>PSP: charges.create (idem-key K-charge)
    Note over P,PSP: network times out — no response reaches P
    P--xC: (response lost)

    Note over C: retry with the SAME key K
    C->>P: POST /payments (key K)
    P->>I: INSERT key K ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    alt existing row COMPLETED
        I-->>P: conflict, cached response
        P-->>C: 200 same transaction_id (no re-charge)
    else existing row IN_PROGRESS
        I-->>P: conflict, in progress
        P-->>C: 409 request_in_progress (retry later)
    end

visuals.caption: 3. PSP Integration (Stripe/Adyen)
visuals.source:
sequenceDiagram participant P as Payment Service participant DB as Postgres (txn + idem + ledger) participant PSP as PSP P->>DB: TXN 1 — write idem row (IN_PROGRESS) + transaction (PENDING) Note over P,DB: commit before PSP call — never hold a txn across the round trip P->>PSP: charges.create (idem-key = transaction_id-charge) alt 2xx success PSP-->>P: charge succeeded P->>DB: TXN 2 — status AUTHORIZED/CAPTURED, write ledger entries, idem COMPLETED else 4xx hard failure PSP-->>P: declined P->>DB: TXN 2 — status FAILED, idem COMPLETED (failure payload) else 5xx or timeout PSP--xP: no clear answer Note over P,DB: leave PENDING + idem IN_PROGRESS
webhook + PENDING-recovery worker finalize later end

visuals.caption: 5. Reconciliation and Settlement
visuals.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant J as Reconciliation Job
    participant PSP as PSP Report API
    participant L as Local Ledger
    participant E as reconciliation_exceptions
    participant O as Ops

    J->>PSP: pull prior-day balance transactions
    PSP-->>J: authoritative payment records
    loop each PSP record
        J->>L: look up transaction by psp_charge_id
        J->>J: compare state, amount, fees, currency
        alt match
            J->>J: OK
        else discrepancy
            J->>E: emit MISSING_LOCAL / MISSING_PSP / AMOUNT_MISMATCH / STATUS_MISMATCH
        end
    end
    J->>J: auto-heal common cases (re-fire own webhook handler)
    alt drift > 0.01% of volume
        E->>O: P1 page
    else unresolved cases
        E->>O: escalate to ops
    end

visuals.caption: Handling Offline Clients
visuals.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as Client (Reconnects)
    participant CS as Chat Server
    participant IT as Inbox Table
    participant MT as Message Table
    
    Client->>CS: Connect (userId)
    CS->>IT: SELECT * FROM Inbox WHERE userId = ?
    IT-->>CS: [msg1, msg2, msg3]
    
    loop For each message ID
        CS->>MT: SELECT * FROM Message WHERE msgId = ?
        MT-->>CS: Message content
        CS->>Client: newMessage(content)
        Client-->>CS: ACK
        CS->>IT: DELETE FROM Inbox WHERE msgId = ?
    end
    
    Note over Client,CS: Client is now in sync
